title: Sequence length queueing & backpressure SKU sweep
content:
Summary:
This doc captures an exploratory sweep comparing how long-context workloads (2k-32k tokens) interact with the serving runtime scheduler and host/GPU interconnect characteristics across three representative cloud SKUs (A100, H100, L40s). The intent was to isolate queueing/backpressure behavior that amplifies tail latency under mixed short+long workloads and to identify mitigations we can apply in the runtime (scheduling, batching, cache handling) and infra (GPU placement, NIC/NVLink affinity).

Why this felt necessary:
- Many previous SKU experiments measured per-GPU throughput and kernel efficiency in isolation, but production traffic mixes short (<=512) and very long (>8k) requests which changes packing and queueing dynamics.
- We observed intermittent tail-latency spikes in customer environments correlated with long-context bursts. This sweep tries to recreate and profile that effect across hardware and driver combinations.

Test matrix (high level):
- Models: redwood-7b-v1 (FP16), redwood-14b-q4 (int8-gguf).
- Sequence lengths: 512, 2048, 8192, 32768 (generation-only load; no tool-calls).
- Concurrency pattern: 80% short (512), 20% long (variable per run) mixed Poisson arrival; separate runs with 100% long for baseline.
- Batch sizing: dynamic continuous batching with max batch 32 tokens/slot, but allowed packing across requests when prefixes match.
- SKUs: AWS p4d (A100 40GB), GCP a3/h100-equivalent (H100 80GB), Azure L40s (L40s 48GB).
- Drivers/CUDA: tested driver stacks that customers are using: CUDA 11.8 + driver 525, CUDA 12.1 + driver 535, CUDA 12.2 + driver 545.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 latency, scheduler queue length over time, per-GPU SM utilization, NVLink/PCIe device-to-device transfer rates, GPU memory fragmentation (free segments), KV cache hit ratio, CPU-side enqueue/dequeue time.

Quick findings (TL;DR):
- H100 hosts consistently had the best tail behavior for long-context mixes; p99 improved by ~20–35% vs A100 and ~30–45% vs L40s for same synthetic traffic.
- L40s showed large variance: single-host throughput at 8k looked competitive, but under mixed arrivals queue depth spiked and p99 increased 2.5x when bursts of long requests arrived. Root cause trace points to elevated PCIe host-to-device stall times during background DMA + NVLink fallback for some host topologies.
- A100 is predictable but has lower single-request gen throughput at extremely long sequences vs H100 (expected). However, A100 runs had more frequent scheduler queue growth because longer kernels take longer to release slots; this amplifies packing delays for pending short requests.
- CUDA/driver stack mattered for L40s more than H100: 12.1/535 produced fewer DMA stalls vs 12.2/545 on the tested L40s images. We think there are driver-level changes in the DMA scatter/gather path affecting concurrent small/large DMA mixes.

Representative numbers (mixed 80% short / 20% 8k long, redwood-7b-v1):
- H100 (CUDA 12.2): p50=32ms, p95=110ms, p99=220ms.
- A100 (CUDA 11.8): p50=38ms, p95=145ms, p99=300ms.
- L40s (CUDA 12.2): p50=45ms, p95=240ms, p99=680ms (with driver 545); with driver 535 p99 dropped to ~340ms.
- Observed queue length at p99 events: typical scheduler queue length grew from baseline 3->12 pending requests on L40s driver 545 runs.

Profiling traces & root causes (notes):
- Host-side enqueue latency rose sharply on L40s when concurrent host DMA was above ~1.2GB/s. The runtime's batch packer waits for KV-slot availability; when the host DMA stalls, the packer shifts to waiting leading to head-of-line blocking for short requests.
- NVLink utilization: H100 showed stable D2D NVLink streaming for KV caches, while L40s deployments with heterogeneous PCIe/NVLink topology had fallback paths that increased latencies for long context warmups.
- GPU-side: long-context generation increases KV cache pressure and causes more frequent cache growth operations. On A100 these cache growths are slower (kernel-side memory allocation patterns), so slots are held longer.
- Driver sensitivity: switching L40s from driver 545 -> 535 reduced host DMA stalls in our environment. We suspect a change in memory registration or scatter/gather handling introduced regressions in 545 for our kernel mix.

Implications for runtime & infra (practical):
1) Scheduler: implement early-ack for short requests when a long request is currently in active generation but the short request can be handled via cached prefix or a small-prefetch path. This avoids head-of-line blocking without violating generation correctness.
2) Prefork long-context workers: isolate long-context requests on a small pool of dedicated GPUs (or dedicated queue slots) to prevent them from monopolizing general-purpose runners. This is especially helpful on A100 clusters.
3) Dynamic preemption thresholds: if queue length > X and average short-request latency exceeds p95 target, favor quick-start path (smaller max batch cap) to prioritize short requests.
4) Driver pinning guidance: recommend L40s customers pin to driver 535/CUDA 12.1 until we've validated 545 at scale (INF-3421 tracking).
5) KV cache eviction heuristics: make warmup less blocking by performing async cache growth in parallel where possible and using optimistic placeholder slots for in-flight growth.

Short-term experiments to validate mitigations (todo):
- Run same mixed workload with "dedicated long-context pool" turned on (fixed 2 GPUs reserved) across all three SKUs and measure p99 changes. (owner: Daniel)
- Implement and A/B the early-ack heuristic in a local runtime branch; measure microbenchmarks for correctness/regression on non-mixed workloads. (owner: Priya)
- Re-run L40s driver matrix including 12.0, 12.1, 12.2, and a 12.3 staging driver to surface the regression gate. Log DMA stall metrics more granularly. (owner: Marco)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is the L40s driver behavior specific to the cloud vendor image (kernel + iommu settings) or a wider driver regression? We need a baremetal test to confirm.
- How much of the A100 scheduler queue amplification is due to kernel-side blocking vs our batcher policy? A narrower microbenchmark that projects kernel hold times should help.
- For multi-tenant Dedicated customers, what's the right tradeoff between isolating long-context pools and utilization efficiency? We need a simulation with realistic traffic traces.

Appendix: short raw traces (snippets):
- sample event stream around a 99th percentile spike (timestamps coarse):
  14:12:03.112 enqueue req-id=abc (short,512)
  14:12:03.115 dequeue req-id=xyz (long,8k) kernel-start
  14:12:03.330 long-kernel dma start->nvlink stream
  14:12:03.421 enqueue req-id=def (short,512)
  14:12:03.422 packer: waiting kv slot for def (held by xyz)
  14:12:03.990 host-dma stall detected (pci-dma wg)
  14:12:04.012 p99 spike observed for def = 880ms

- config used for benchmark harness:
  - serving-runtime commit: abc1234 (benchmark branch: long-context-queueing-sweep)
  - runner config flags: --max-batch=32 --kv-cache-priority=balanced --prefetch=auto --early-ack=false (toggled in later runs)

Notes for docs/next steps:
- Add this as a follow-up section to the long-context ops confluence page and link PRs (INF-3421).
- Capture baremetal L40s results (request infra help).
- Prioritize early-ack patch for small scale canary after QA signoff.

Rough conclusion: long-context workloads expose scheduler and PCIe/NVLink interplay in ways that single-request benchmarks miss. H100's interconnect and kernel improvements make it more robust under mixed traffic; L40s shows the biggest sensitivity to driver versions and host topology. Short-term mitigations in the runtime scheduler (early-ack, dedicated long-context pools, adaptive batching) plus driver pinning guidance for L40s should materially reduce customer-observed tail spikes while we continue root-cause work.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- capture raw nvlink monitor logs and attach to INF-3421 before next weekly eng sync.
- ask infra to repro with iommu off.
- circle back to research on async KV growth pattern we prototyped (felt promising on H100).
